justification: The shape-C skeleton is sound and matches the plan row: simple factory (unnamed pattern) -> Factory Method -> Abstract Factory -> Builder -> Builder in the BCL (StringBuilder, WebApplicationBuilder) -> Singleton via Lazy<T> -> what a global singleton costs tests -> the DI lifetime that replaced it. That is a genuine comparison/decision arc, not a bag of unrelated sections, and each of the three creation-flow diagrams required by the brief is present, captioned, theme-aware via the class system, and portrait (340 wide, well under the 360 cap) -- Figure 1 for Factory Method, Figure 2 for Builder, Figure 3 for Singleton/Lazy<T>. Code fences are all correctly tagged per the run-code.mjs table, xUnit blocks correctly wildcard only the version banner and Time value, and the two 'fails' xUnit blocks (a genuinely-red test demonstrating the Singleton coupling bug, and a deliberately engineered red-to-green pair) are used exactly as the writer guide's TDD-red convention describes. However, two concrete defects keep this out of 8.5+ territory. First, the exercise 'Find the missing guarantee' (lines 463-468) contains a duplicated setup: line 464 introduces the LazyThreadSafetyMode.None rewrite and ends with a colon that promises a code block or continuation, but instead line 466 restates the identical setup in a second, differently-worded sentence ('This rewrite of AppConfiguration replaces LazyThreadSafetyMode.ExecutionAndPublication with LazyThreadSafetyMode.None...') before the actual question appears on line 468. This reads as an unedited draft artifact -- two competing versions of the same sentence left in -- and no page at the MDN/Real Python bar would ship a visibly duplicated paragraph in the middle of an exercise prompt; a reader hits redundant, slightly contradictory framing exactly where the article is asking them to reason carefully. Second, a mobile-clipping problem sits on the single line of code the surrounding prose and the next exercise are both about: `new(() => new AppConfiguration(), LazyThreadSafetyMode.ExecutionAndPublication);` (md line 413, inside the id=lazy-singleton block) is 8-space-indented plus 82 characters of content -- 90 columns total -- and the token `LazyThreadSafetyMode.ExecutionAndPublication` itself does not start until column ~43, past the ~40-column visible boundary the writer guide sets for a 390px phone. The writer guide is explicit that the operative part of a line must stay on screen when the prose is about it, and here the very next exercise interrogates exactly this argument (None vs ExecutionAndPublication); a phone reader has to scroll the code block sideways to see the thing the article and the exercise are both discussing. The declaration was already split across two lines (field decl, then `new(...)`), which is the right instinct, but the second line is still too long. Diagram quality itself is strong (all three pass every hard-rule check I could verify statically) with only cosmetic nits: Figure 1's 'resolved by the runtime type' annotation (line 166) is prose, not code, but is styled with the `d-mono` class alongside genuinely code-ish siblings like 'calls CreateWriter()' on the line above, whereas Figures 2 and 3 correctly reserve `d-mono` for literal code/API names and use plain `d-small d-muted` for prose annotations -- a minor inconsistency in an otherwise well-executed set. Code/readability formatting is otherwise clean: no fence violates run-code.mjs conventions, no `text output` block is misplaced, paragraphs are dense but not unbroken walls of text (the longest run ~150 words, broken up by inline quotations and code identifiers), and the three exercises correctly keep predict-the-output-style leaks out of view (none of the three shows output under the question; all solutions are properly collapsed in `:::solution`). Exercise variety is thinner than ideal -- all three are 'explain the reasoning' prose questions (none is extend-the-code, measure-it, or predict-the-output), which is a minor miss against the brief's 'vary their form' guidance but not by itself a design/UX blocker.
